source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in LLMs (framing by scenario)
finding: Frontier models incl. reasoning models (o3, Claude Sonnet 4 with thinking) show the classic loss-frame risk seeking only in some narrative scenarios. The sign and size of the framing effect depends on the scenario wording, not on whether the model reasons.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-4o, o3, Claude Sonnet 4 with and without thinking, Gemini 1.5 Pro), 25 runs per condition, 2,550 decisions (2.3% unparsed, dropped), 3-option items with equal EV 0.5. Championship: loss frame BLITZ 85.6% vs gain frame 0.8%; gain frame CONTROL 88.8%. Framing effect size (loss minus gain mean risk score, 0-2 scale) +1.40 to +1.84 across 5 models. Career transition reversed in all 5 models: loss frame safe APPLY 87.2% vs 41.6% in gain frame (effect -0.37 to -0.60). Business merger near zero (-0.24 to +0.12).
limits: Single author, three-option items (not the 1979 problems), hypothetical, LLM-coded rationales, temperature not stated in the text read. Mann-Whitney tests per scenario, no correction stated. Gemini 2.5 Pro excluded because it refused military items.
agent_relevance: Frame effects survive reasoning mode and are scenario-specific, so a scaffold cannot assume a thinking model is frame-proof (guardrail on wording sensitivity).

source: Payne (2025) math-form control and forced-choice follow-up
finding: When the same equal-EV problem is written as pure symbolic maths, framing effects vanish: both GPT-4o and o3 compute the EVs and declare indifference. If forced to pick one option, both always pick the risk-free one.
numbers: Free-choice maths condition: o3 200/200 (100%) declared indifference; GPT-4o 196/200 (98%). Forced choice: every single time the risk-free option. Text says o3 computed EV correctly about 85% of the time in the military narratives yet still showed framing there. Framing effect size not correlated with how often a model calculated EV (Fig. 2).
limits: Only 2 models in the maths control; the neutral wording also removes the narrative cues, so it cannot separate re-expression from removing context. Author reads it as language-embedded bias; not tested against other accounts. Tie-breaking toward the sure option is an artefact of the forced-choice rule.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 2: re-expressing a story as plain final-outcome maths removes the flip in o3 and GPT-4o. It was not compared with chain of thought at equal tokens.

source: Payne (2025) EV-calculation rates by scenario type
finding: Models calculated expected value much more often in civilian than in military scenarios, and GPT-4o rarely calculated it anywhere. Calculating EV is not what removed the frame effect.
numbers: Two LLM coders (Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o) agreed with Cohen's kappa 0.9354 (civilian) and 0.9249 (military). Per-scenario EV-calculation percentages are in Table 7 but the layout was scrambled in text extraction, so only the direction is recorded here.
limits: Correlational. The text itself says calculating EV correlates with an aggregate dampening of the framing effect in one place and limited correlation in another.
agent_relevance: Asking for an EV computation is not the same as neutralising the frame. The operator needs to rewrite the problem, not just add a calculation step.

source: Ge, Zhang and Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) gap: risky choices of reasoning vs conversational LLMs (clusters)
finding: 20 LLMs split into reasoning models (RMs) and conversational models (CMs). RMs track an expected-payoff maximiser, ignore option order and gain/loss framing, and behave about the same with stated probabilities or sampled histories. CMs are order- and frame-sensitive.
numbers: 360 Prolific humans; 20 LLMs; 324 questions per model (6 explicit + 48 implicit, x2 orders, x3 explanation modes), 10 queries each at T=1, three base prospect pairs. Correlation with expected-payoff maximiser: RMs (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-2.5-Pro) 0.86 to 1.0; CMs below 0.5; humans 0.14. Highest LLM-human correlation 0.42 (Claude-4.5-Haiku). Math-trained vs instruct twins: Qwen2.5-Math-7B 1.00 vs Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 0.64; Olmo-3-7B-Think 1.00 vs Instruct 0.73.
limits: Few base prospect pairs; not the K&T 1979 items; no direct certainty, reflection or isolation tests. Numbers taken from the arXiv v2 page summary plus the ACL PDF text. Models mostly 2025 vintage.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 1: current reasoning models are close to EV-maximisers on simple gambles. Not a verbatim test of the 1979 items.

source: Ge et al. (2026) description-history gap, 20 vs 100 draws
finding: Every model moves toward human-like and away from EV-like choice when prospects are shown as outcome histories. The gap is modest for frontier RMs, large for frontier CMs, and large again for small open RMs. A longer history (100 draws) does not remove it.
numbers: Histories of 20 and 100 simulated payoffs; the paper says many LLMs behave more rationally with 100 than with 20 (Appendix C, not in the text I read). Context length ruled out: DeepSeek-Chat has a 128K window, 100 samples is a small fraction. Open RMs: the 30B/32B models show sharper shifts than 7B. Implicit-prospect correlation with the EV agent: GPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-R1 0.98, Gemini-Pro 0.94, CMs 0.45-0.58, humans 0.53.
limits: Per-model 20-vs-100 numbers sit in an appendix I could not open; size by model class is only described in words and arrows on a plot. Humans became more EV-like with histories, an oddity the authors note. Not the classic Hertwig paradigm (no rare-event underweighting test).
agent_relevance: Closes gap 3 in direction (gap exists for all classes, smallest for frontier RMs) but not in per-model size. If an agent learns risk from simulated draws, expect CMs to drift from EV.

source: Ge et al. (2026) explanation (rationale) conditions
finding: Asking for a short explanation often moves CMs toward EV-like choice, but asking for a math explanation often does the opposite. RMs are mostly stable.
numbers: GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-R1, Olmo3-7B-think and Qwen2.5-Math-7B show strong stability; Gemini-2.5-Pro looks like a CM; Qwen3-30B-Thinking and Olmo3-32B-Think change a lot under math explanation. Claude-4.5-Haiku moves away from EV under both explanation types. Authors: asking for a longer rationale often reduces decision rationality for CMs.
limits: The explanation is requested alongside the choice, so this is not a chain-of-thought-before-answer manipulation, and token counts are not equated.
agent_relevance: More words from a conversational model do not mean less bias. Weakly relevant to gap 2: a verbose rewrite is not enough; the rewrite has to strip the frame.

source: Yechiam and Tarabeih (2026) Mimicry without understanding (Studies 1-3)
finding: ChatGPT-4o and Qwen copy the loss-aversion level they are told humans showed, even from a tiny fictitious sample. Mimicry does not depend on how representative the human sample is.
numbers: Study 3: described human preference (loss averse vs gain seeking) on accept rate B=17.92, p<.001; sample size (n=43 vs 10,583) B=0.13, p=.50; interaction B=-0.09, p=.75. Fitted lambda: ChatGPT 1.257/1.218 when told humans were loss averse vs 1.072 when gain seeking; Qwen 1.742 vs 0.940/0.929. Effect larger at -$5/+$6 than at -$6/+$6 (B=1.46, p<.001 for ChatGPT).
limits: Two models only; lambda computed from accept/reject at a few lottery points; effects strongest where the bias is cheap in EV. Hypothetical gambles. A coauthor also wrote the Tarabeih meta-analysis (not independent).
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to gap 4: text the agent reads can move its own risk attitude. A reading agent needs a guardrail against copying reported bias levels.

source: Yechiam and Tarabeih (2026) Study 4a/4b: real meta-analysis abstracts and full papers
finding: Prompting with the abstract or full text of a loss-aversion paper moves the model's lambda in line with the paper's reported human lambda, even though the papers call it a bias.
numbers: Papers: Brown et al. (lambda 1.96, 150 studies), Walasek et al. (1.31, 17 studies), Yechiam and Zeif (1.07). 4a abstracts: ChatGPT lambda 1.785 (Brown) down to 1.043 (Yechiam and Zeif); Qwen 1.170 to 1.047; chi2(7)=1,043, r2=0.58; ChatGPT accepted 105% more lotteries after Yechiam and Zeif than after Brown, Qwen 9% more. 4b full text (ChatGPT only; Qwen text too long): lambda 1.519 (Brown) vs 1.082 (Yechiam and Zeif); chi2(3)=313, r2=0.33, 51% more acceptance. No-paper control about 1.09 for ChatGPT.
limits: The paper sits in the same context as the choice, which is stronger than an agent reading a paper many steps earlier. Only 2 models. Authors favour the loss aversion is weak view (Yechiam and Zeif is their own paper).
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 4 for same-context priming. No test of delayed priming inside a long agent run.

source: Yechiam and Tarabeih (2026) joint-evaluation debiasing test
finding: Re-running Study 2 with all six lotteries judged together (instead of one at a time) shrank the effect of the described human behaviour, except where loss aversion did not conflict with EV.
numbers: ChatGPT agents answered accept/reject for lotteries A-F in one prompt. The difference between conditions appeared only when gains equalled losses. No effect size in the main text; details are in the supplement, which I did not open.
limits: Single model, supplement only, no numbers read. Authors say proper design of prompts and algorithms may substantially reduce the tendency.
agent_relevance: First evidence that a guardrail (compare alternatives jointly) reduces the priming effect. Only part of gap 4's can-a-guardrail-remove-it question.

source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect theory in LLMs: meta-analysis (training, release year, base vs tuned)
finding: Between-model spread in lambda is huge, so no single LLM profile exists. Holding family fixed, lambda falls with release year. The paper cannot say whether training data, tuning or safety objectives cause it.
numbers: Pooled lambda 1.26 [1.06, 1.46] (102 estimates, 32 models); GPT-3.5 2.72 vs GPT-4.1 0.57; release year -0.16 per year within family; asymmetric designs (loss smaller than gain) pooled 1.46 [0.96, 1.96] vs human about 2.3 (t=-3.81, p=.004), symmetric designs 1.15 [0.98, 1.32] vs human 1.07 (t=0.79, p=.44). Probability weighting 0.81 [0.65, 0.98] under T&K, 0.65 for studies without Ge et al.; reasoning and conversational models not different (three share 0.81); curvature near linear (1.01). Egger p=.58, Begg p=.37.
limits: Author coauthored one of the pooled studies. Designs confounded with models. Several fits hit the upper bound of the choice-sensitivity parameter. No matched base-vs-tuned lambda contrast exists in the pool.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for lambda. The agent should treat LLM loss aversion as design- and model-specific.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld and Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias (certainty effect, base vs tuned)
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF raise the certainty effect: pretrained bases show almost none, tuned versions show clear bias. This is the only matched base-versus-tuned comparison on a K&T item that I found.
numbers: Certainty-effect bias score (target-choice rate in treatment minus control): pretrained GPT-3 DaVinci 0.00, T5 0.09, Mistral 0.03; tuned DaVinci-002 0.24, DaVinci-003 0.67, Flan-T5 0.17, Mistral-Instruct 0.29. Authors: RLHF (002 to 003) amplifies, and instruction tuning alone (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct) suffices.
limits: Certainty items are product-choice templates (not the 1979 wording); table layout partly garbled, so only the values the authors list in prose were used. Old models (2023). No loss-aversion lambda.
agent_relevance: Supports tuning, not just data, for the certainty effect only. Does not answer the lambda question in gap 8.

source: Wang et al. (2025/2026) Rethinking prospect theory for LLMs (fit stability across models)
finding: Fitted prospect-theory parameters scatter widely across 7 LLMs and several fits sit at the optimiser boundary, so lambda is not a stable trait. Decoding temperature was fixed at 0.7 and not varied.
numbers: Table 2 (alpha, lambda, gamma; human Tanaka values 0.670, 2.630, 0.685): Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct lambda 0.010 (boundary), Qwen2.5-7B 0.010 (boundary), Mistral-7B 0.570, Qwen2.5-14B 1.909, Qwen2.5-32B 1.213, Gemini-2.5-Flash 1.499, GPT-5-Mini 4.000. 256 samples per lottery question, 35 questions, history length 10, T=0.7. Reliable-fit rule MAE <= 0.20 and R2 >= 0.10.
limits: No temperature sweep and no repeat-run (test-retest) analysis; speaks to between-model instability only. GPT-5-Mini and Gemini-Flash ran with CoT but expected-value calculation was forbidden.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: between-model spread is large (0.01 to 4.0). Direct test-retest for one fixed model is not done here.

source: Yee and Koh (2026) LLMs as calibrated measurement instruments for behavioural parameters (temperature, repeat stability)
finding: Baseline LLM loss aversion is low and a loss-averse profile prompt raises it above the human value. Estimates are stable at T up to 0.7 and noisy at T=1.0. Probability weighting was unreliable across repeats.
numbers: 4 models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Gemini-2.5-Pro), 19,200 agent-scenario pairs (24,000 with an excluded Gemini-2.5-Flash). Baseline lambda 1.12 under a rational profile (range 1.12-1.90 across baselines) vs human 2.25; loss-averse profile 3.00 (+1.88, d=1.82). Temperature grid 0, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0: coefficient of variation < 0.15 for T <= 0.7, > 0.30 at T=1.0. Probability weighting intra-class correlation 0.62 (below usual reliability thresholds). GPT-4o (June 2024) vs GPT-4 (March 2024) correlation > 0.85 on all parameters. Gamble-based lambda correlates 0.42 with disposition-implied lambda.
limits: Short appendix paragraphs carry the stability claims; single research group preprint; synthetic financial scenarios; profile prompts are the manipulation. Old model versions (2024).
agent_relevance: Best available answer to gap 9: lambda is fairly repeatable at T<=0.7 for a fixed model and prompt, probability weighting is not. A single-run lambda for an agent is not trustworthy beyond that.

source: Hashimoto, Takayanagi, Suzuki and Izumi (2025) Agent-based market simulation with LLM traders (reference-point shifts)
finding: LLM trading agents change buy/sell choices when the reference point shifts from the purchase price to a past peak or trough, in a loss-averse, reference-dependent way. Some models do it, others do not.
numbers: Single-turn test, 100 trials per cell (seeded), purchase price 300, cash 30,000. Net order flow (buys, sells): GPT-4o G+ -94 (3, 97), G- -70 (15, 85), L- +80 (90, 10), L+ +74 (87, 13); Llama-3.1-8B -80, -74, +86, +60; Qwen-2.5-7B G+ -72 (14, 86), G- -68 (16, 84). Qwen kept selling to realise gains even after a fall from the peak, unlike GPT-4o and Llama. Multi-step: 500 simulated days; the LLM agents reproduced the price-falls-near-all-time-high anomaly that rule-based agents could not.
limits: Qwen row of Table 4 read from garbled layout. Disposition-style behaviour is a reference-point effect but not a lambda estimate. No human control. Models are 2024 vintage.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 7 in part: reference-point sensitivity shows in agent settings with context, and varies by model. The agent should state its reference point explicitly.

source: Li et al. (2026) Behavioural consistency validation for LLM agents: trading-style switching
finding: In year-long stock simulations, agents prompted with strong loss aversion switch trading style less than weak-loss-aversion agents in all four models, but the other drivers (herding, wealth, misalignment) align poorly.
numbers: 4 LLMs, 16 strong-loss-aversion vs 16 weak agents per comparison. Mann-Whitney U: GPT-4o-mini 214.0, p=.0003, rank-biserial 0.67; Gemini 201.0, p=.002, 0.51; DeepSeek 195.0, p=.004, 0.47; Qwen 201.0, p=.002, 0.51. Herding significant only for Qwen (p=.04); a rule-based ABM aligns on all four drivers.
limits: Loss aversion is a prompted personality trait, not a measured choice pattern, so alignment partly measures instruction following. Small groups of 16.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a prompted loss-averse persona changes multi-step behaviour in the expected direction. It does not show natural reference-dependence.

source: Marks and Vollberg (2026) The psychophysics of affect in large language models
finding: Current models follow expected value almost perfectly in simple gambles and show weak, inconsistent loss aversion. Predicted feelings show the reverse asymmetry (gains feel stronger than losses) that vanishes when outcomes are rated together.
numbers: 10 LLMs (incl. gpt-5.2, grok-4.3, gemini-3-flash, kimi-k2.5, claude-sonnet-4.5); 30 simulated participants per condition. Higher-EV gamble taken on 94.3-99.9% of trials by gpt-5-nano, gpt-5.2, grok-4.3, gemini-3-flash, kimi-k2.5; claude-sonnet-4.5 83.5%; llama-3.1-70b 73.0%; gpt-4o-mini took the lower-EV gamble 53.6% of the time. At equal EV most took the sure option (gamble 10.8-38.1%). Lambda 0.88-1.59 across models; kimi-k2.5 1.07-1.28; gpt-5-nano 1.005-1.04. Gain scale larger than loss scale in 8 of 9 models (+1.2 to +24.3). Stock task: ratings linearise single 0.26-0.43, memory 0.52-0.68, joint 0.98-0.99.
limits: Ratings task is not a classic choice test; only two focal models in all conditions; hypothetical; the first author works at a bank (stated in the paper).
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partial: 2025-26 models are close to EV and weakly loss averse on gambles. Gap 2 hint: joint comparison linearises the value mapping.

source: Hintze, Bisht, Schossau and Hertwig (2025) Nonlinear transformation of probabilities by LLMs (Research Square preprint)
finding: LLMs mostly do not show the human inverse-S probability weighting. GPT-3.5 was risk seeking, Claude 3.0 showed strong recency, and GPT-4 underweighted small and overweighted large probabilities, like humans deciding from experience rather than from description.
numbers: Abstract only: sure outcome vs two-outcome lottery tasks; no per-model parameters read.
limits: Abstract read through Crossref, full text not opened. Old models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude 3).
agent_relevance: Relevant to gap 6: LLM weighting curves look like an experience pattern, which fits a complexity or heuristic account but does not test it.

source: Oprea (2024) Decisions under risk are decisions under complexity, American Economic Review
finding: Probability-weighting and loss-aversion anomalies also appear when payments are deterministic but disaggregated to look like lotteries, so they may be complexity errors, not risk preferences.
numbers: Abstract: anomalies arise with equal strength in deterministic tasks and correlate across subjects with the same anomalies in lotteries. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Only the abstract was read this session. A 2025 SSRN reply by Li, Liu, Niu and Wang titled Decisions Under Risk are not Decisions Under Complexity disputes it (title and authors only; no abstract available to me).
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: I found no LLM test of the mirror (no-risk) pattern. The idea that LLM weighting is a complexity heuristic is untested.

source: Wulff, Mergenthaler-Canseco and Hertwig (2018) A meta-analytic review of two modes of learning and the description-experience gap
finding: The description-experience gap is robust but depends on problem structure. The biggest driver is small samples, but the gap persists when sampling error is almost removed.
numbers: More than 70,000 choices from more than 6,000 participants in the sampling paradigm. Recency appeared only when people chose when to stop (optional stopping). Different probability weighting found only when the problem has a risky and a safe option.
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex); effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the effect-size detail is still missing, but the structure moderator matters for how LLM history tasks (explicit gamble vs safe) are built.

source: Gal and Rucker (2018) The loss of loss aversion: will it loom larger than its gain? Journal of Consumer Psychology
finding: Review concluding that current evidence does not support losses being more impactful than gains on balance. Also argues belief in loss aversion persists for reasons of scientific belief maintenance.
numbers: Abstract: no effect sizes.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref). Review, not new data; stakes are not discussed in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: supports the conditional-not-universal reading, consistent with LLM lambda varying by design.

source: Yechiam (2019) Acceptable losses: the debatable origins of loss aversion, Psychological Research
finding: Review: early utility-function studies found that very large losses are overweighted but small losses often are not, and some findings were misread as loss aversion, including K&T 1979 evidence.
numbers: Abstract only: no numbers.
limits: Abstract via Europe PMC; the small-stake argument is the relevant part for hypothetical LLM gambles.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: small hypothetical stakes are where human loss aversion is weakest, so a near-1 LLM lambda is not odd.

source: SSRN 7174959 (2026) Framing moves the paradox: concrete numbers attenuate the Allais certainty effect
finding: A boundary condition on the certainty effect in humans: showing probabilities as identifiable events (a 00-99 lottery draw) shrinks the Allais pattern.
numbers: Preference shift for the safe option between Problems 1 and 2: -39 percentage points with percentages vs -12 with numbers; difference-in-differences z=2.34, p=.019; logistic interaction p=.032.
limits: Abstract only; working paper, not peer reviewed; sample size not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 hint: a concrete re-expression of probabilities weakens the certainty effect in people, so the re-expression operator has a human precedent.

source: Tversky and Kahneman (1992) weighting parameters as used by Tarabeih (2026) Table S1
finding: The 1992 benchmark for probability weighting used in the LLM meta-analysis is 0.65. This is consistent with gamma 0.61 (gains) and delta 0.69 (losses) averaging to 0.65, but the primary 1992 text was not obtained.
numbers: Tarabeih: original estimates of Tversky and Kahneman (1992), alpha = 0.88 and gamma = 0.65 (Table S1). Mean of 0.61 and 0.69 is 0.65.
limits: Indirect: equating 0.65 with the average of 0.61 and 0.69 is my arithmetic. The 1992 PDFs I tried (CMU, KTH, DTIC, ResearchGate) were not retrievable and Brown et al. does not list gamma and delta.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 is only partly closed.
